title: How to Know If You Need a Specialist Architect for Your Project
excerpt: Not every renovation needs an architect, but some projects definitely do. Here's how to tell if your Westchester home needs one.
content:
You're thinking about adding a second story to your home in Scarsdale. Or maybe you want to open up your kitchen in Mamaroneck. Either way, you're wondering: do I really need an architect for this, or can I just hire a contractor and figure it out as we go?

That's a smart question to ask before you start. The honest answer is that some projects need a licensed architect in Westchester, NY and some don't. But if you guess wrong, you could end up with permits denied, unsafe construction, or work that has to be torn out and redone.

When a Contractor Alone Isn't Enough

A lot of homeowners assume that any good general contractor can handle any job. That's not how it works. In New York State, certain types of work legally require an architect's involvement. If your project involves structural changes to your home, you need someone who understands load-bearing walls, foundation work, and how buildings actually stay standing.

Home additions in Westchester often fall into this category. Adding a second story or expanding your footprint means new foundation work, new roof lines, and new structural systems. A licensed architect in New York is trained to design these systems safely and make sure they meet code. A general contractor can build what you give them, but they're not licensed to design structural systems from scratch.

Historic restorations are another area where you need real expertise. Many homes in towns like Bronxville and Pelham Manor were built decades ago with materials and methods that aren't used anymore. Restoring them properly requires understanding the original construction and making sure any new work respects the building's integrity while meeting modern code.

Permitting and Your Local Building Department

Every Westchester municipality has its own building department that reviews plans before construction can start. In Rye, Hastings-on-Hudson, and Tarrytown, that review process is thorough and it should be. Building inspectors are looking for architectural stamped drawings on anything structural or substantial. When a licensed architect prepares your plans, the building department takes that seriously because they know someone with real liability insurance designed the work.

Without architectural drawings, your contractor has to work from sketches or rough ideas. The building department might reject those plans outright, which means you're back to square one.

Design-Build Firms Handle Both Sides

One way to make sure you get both design and construction right is to work with a design-build firm where the same person does both the architecture and the construction. Silvio M. Luca runs House Architecture & Construction as both a licensed architect and general contractor based in Eastchester. He personally oversees every project, which means the design that gets drawn is the design that actually gets built. No miscommunication between two different companies. No finger-pointing if something goes wrong.

This matters especially on complex work like primary suite additions in places like White Plains or New Rochelle, or kitchen remodels in Harrison where you're dealing with plumbing, electrical, structural changes, and finishes all at once.

When You Should Call an Architect

Bottom line: call an architect if you're adding square footage, moving walls, changing your roof, dealing with an older home, or if anyone has hinted that your project needs permits. A custom home in Westchester County definitely needs one. So does a basement conversion or a major kitchen renovation where you're moving walls.

Small cosmetic work like painting, cabinet refacing, or replacing fixtures? A good contractor handles that fine on their own. But anything structural, anything that touches the building's bones, anything that affects how it sits on the foundation or how it sheds water needs professional design.
